mcqs.q: The word 'tomography' literally means:
mcqs.explain: Tomo = slice, graphia = writing; tomography images one section/layer while blurring the others.

mcqs.q: Computed tomography (CT) was introduced in 1967 by:
mcqs.explain: Sir Godfrey Hounsfield introduced CT scanning in 1967; the CT density unit (Hounsfield unit) is named after him.

mcqs.q: In a CT scanner, the rotating gantry houses the:
opts: X-ray tube and the detectors, with the patient between them
mcqs.explain: The gantry contains the x-ray tube (rotating anode) and the detectors; the patient lies between the source and detectors, and exposures are taken over a 180–360° arc.

mcqs.q: CT detectors capture the exiting beam using:
opts: Scintillation crystals that emit light, read by a photodetector
mcqs.explain: Scintillation crystals (e.g. gadolinium oxysulfide) emit visible light when struck by x-rays; a photodetector converts the light into an electrical signal.

mcqs.q: On the Hounsfield scale, the CT number for water, dense bone and air are:
mcqs.explain: Hounsfield units: water = 0, dense bone = +1000, air = −1000; these appear as grey shades.

mcqs.q: The contrast agent used in contrast-enhanced CT is iodine, which is:
opts: Given intravenously and toxic in kidney disease and asthmatics
mcqs.explain: Iodine contrast is given IV to enhance soft tissue/vessels but is toxic to patients with kidney disease and asthmatics.

mcqs.q: A key ADVANTAGE of CT over plain radiography is:
opts: Multiplanar imaging (axial, coronal, sagittal) with no overlap of structures
Use of no radiation at all
mcqs.explain: CT eliminates overlap and provides multiplanar (axial/coronal/sagittal) reconstructions; it is ideal for hard tissue.

mcqs.q: A DISADVANTAGE of CT is:
opts: High radiation dose and artifacts from metallic restorations
mcqs.explain: CT delivers a high radiation dose, metal restorations cause artifacts, and its soft-tissue contrast is poorer than MRI.

mcqs.q: CBCT is named 'cone beam' because it:
opts: Uses a cone-shaped beam capturing a large volume in a single rotation
Uses a linear fan beam over many rotations
Uses sound waves in a cone
mcqs.explain: CBCT uses a cone-shaped x-ray beam that captures a large volume in one rotation around the head; conventional CT uses a linear fan beam.

mcqs.q: Compared with medical CT, CBCT delivers a radiation dose that is:
mcqs.explain: CBCT uses up to ~40% less dose than conventional CT (though still more than a regular dental x-ray), with a rapid single-rotation scan.

mcqs.q: Which is a typical indication for CBCT?
opts: Pre-operative assessment of impacted teeth and bone for implants
mcqs.explain: CBCT excels at bony/dental pathology, impacted teeth, TMJ and implant-site bone analysis; it is poor for soft-tissue detail.

mcqs.q: Diagnostic ultrasound uses sound-wave frequencies of:
mcqs.explain: Diagnostic ultrasound uses 1–20 MHz vibrations — far above the audible range (1,500–20,000 Hz).

mcqs.q: On ultrasound, a structure giving NO echoes appears ___ and is termed:
mcqs.explain: Anechoic = no echoes (dark); hyperechoic = strong echoes (bright); hypoechoic = weak echoes (darker).

mcqs.q: A common dental/maxillofacial use of ultrasound is:
opts: Evaluating salivary glands (stones, cysts) and lymph nodes
mcqs.explain: Ultrasound is used for salivary glands, lymph nodes, TMJ/muscle, abscesses and soft-tissue oral lesions — not for bone.

mcqs.q: A major ADVANTAGE of ultrasonography is that it:
opts: Uses no ionizing radiation and is non-invasive
Has very high resolution for deep lesions
mcqs.explain: Ultrasound uses no ionizing radiation, is non-invasive/painless and shows soft-tissue differences well, though it is poor for bone and deep lesions.

mcqs.q: MRI generates images by acting on the body's:
opts: Hydrogen protons, using a strong magnet and radio waves
mcqs.explain: MRI aligns the body's hydrogen protons in a strong magnetic field; an RF pulse displaces them and the released signal forms the image.

mcqs.q: On MRI, which sequence is used mainly to evaluate PATHOLOGY?
mcqs.explain: T1-weighted images show normal anatomy; T2-weighted images are used to evaluate pathology.

mcqs.q: MRI is CONTRAINDICATED in patients with:
mcqs.explain: The strong magnetic field makes MRI unsafe for patients with pacemakers or ferromagnetic implants; claustrophobia and noise are other limitations.

mcqs.q: Which modality is BEST for a TMJ disc disorder or soft-tissue head-and-neck lesion?
mcqs.explain: MRI gives the highest soft-tissue contrast, making it ideal for TMJ disc disorders, salivary glands and soft-tissue H&N pathology.

mcqs.q: The radiotracer most commonly used in PET imaging is:
mcqs.explain: FDG (fluorodeoxyglucose) is the common PET tracer; it concentrates in metabolically active tissue such as cancer cells.

mcqs.q: In a PET scan, the radiotracer emits positrons which:
opts: Collide with electrons to produce gamma rays detected by a gamma camera
mcqs.explain: Positrons collide with electrons, producing gamma rays that a gamma camera detects to build a 3D image of tissue FUNCTION (not just structure).

mcqs.q: PET imaging shows tissue ___, making it valuable for:
mcqs.explain: PET reveals functional/metabolic activity, so it is used to detect, stage and monitor cancer, plus neurological and cardiac assessment.

mcqs.q: Which imaging technique delivers the HIGHEST typical effective dose?
mcqs.explain: A whole-body PET scan (~4000–7000 µSv) gives a far higher dose than a periapical (5–8 µSv), OPG (10–30 µSv) or CBCT.

mcqs.q: Which modality uses NO ionizing radiation?
mcqs.explain: MRI (magnet + radio waves) and ultrasound (sound waves) use no ionizing radiation; CT, CBCT, PET and plain films all do.

saqs.q: Define a CT number (Hounsfield unit) and give the values for bone, water and air.
saqs.a: A value reflecting how much a tissue absorbs x-rays, shown as a grey shade. Bone +1000, water 0, air −1000.

saqs.q: How does CBCT differ from conventional CT, and give one advantage.
saqs.a: CBCT uses a cone beam capturing a volume in one rotation (CT uses a linear fan beam over many). Advantage: lower dose (~40% less), rapid single scan, adjustable FOV.

saqs.q: Define anechoic, hyperechoic and hypoechoic on ultrasound.
saqs.a: Anechoic = no echoes (dark); hyperechoic = strong echoes (bright); hypoechoic = weak echoes (darker).

saqs.q: Explain the basic principle of MRI.
saqs.a: A strong magnet aligns the body's hydrogen protons; a radiofrequency pulse displaces them; when it stops they realign and release a signal that the computer reconstructs into images (T1 anatomy, T2 pathology).
Pacemakers & ferromagnetic implants (unsafe), poor intra-bony imaging, time-consuming, claustrophobia, noisy.

saqs.q: Describe how a PET scan works and its main use.
saqs.a: A radiotracer (FDG) is taken up by metabolically active tissue; it emits positrons → gamma rays detected by a gamma camera, imaging function. Main use: detecting/staging cancer.

saqs.q: Which modalities are best for hard tissue, soft tissue and function respectively?
saqs.a: Hard tissue: CT/CBCT. Soft tissue: MRI / ultrasound (no radiation). Function/metabolism: PET.
